subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram‑negative rod that thrives in moist environments and forms biofilms. It causes opportunistic infections, especially in immunocompromised or device‑bearing patients. Rapid recognition and appropriate antibiotics are essential.

sections.p: P. aeruginosa is a ubiquitous, aerobic, gram‑negative rod with a distinctive grape‑like odor. It is intrinsically resistant to many antibiotics and can form protective biofilms on surfaces and devices.
b: Gram‑negative rod; oxidase positive; motile; produces pyocyanin pigment

sections.p: Its virulence stems from exotoxins, elastases, and a robust biofilm matrix that shields it from host defenses and antibiotics.
b: Biofilm – protects against immune cells and drugs

sections.p: The bacterium survives in water, soil, and hospital sinks. It spreads via contaminated equipment, hands, or environmental surfaces.

P. aeruginosa causes a spectrum of infections: ventilator‑associated pneumonia, catheter‑related bloodstream infections, burn wound sepsis, and ocular infections. In cystic fibrosis, chronic airway colonization leads to progressive lung damage.
Clinical suspicion is followed by culture and susceptibility testing. In low‑resource settings, a simple Gram stain and growth on cetrimide agar can suggest the organism.
b: Sputum or wound culture on cetrimide agar

t.b: Shows gram‑negative rods; suggests Pseudomonas if oxidase positive
Mucoid colonies indicate Pseudomonas; confirms identity when available

sections.p: First treat the source (remove catheters, decontaminate surfaces). Use antipseudomonal beta‑lactams or fluoroquinolones, avoiding agents with poor penetration or high toxicity.
b: Avoid aminoglycosides alone due to nephrotoxicity

t.b: Removal of infected device reduces bacterial load
Check renal function when using nephrotoxic agents

sections.p: Remember that Pseudomonas is a common cause of infection in patients with indwelling devices, burns, or cystic fibrosis. Its biofilm formation explains chronicity and resistance.
Other gram‑negative rods like Acinetobacter or Klebsiella can cause similar hospital infections but lack the characteristic odor and pigment.
b: Acinetobacter – no grape odor; Klebsiella – lactose fermenter

sections.p: Low‑yield cultures in early infection may miss Pseudomonas; a negative Gram stain does not rule it out. Biofilm‑producing strains may show delayed growth.

faq.q: What makes Pseudomonas resistant to many antibiotics?
faq.a: It has efflux pumps, low‑permeability outer membrane, and enzymes that inactivate beta‑lactams.

faq.q: Can it be prevented in hospitals?
faq.a: Strict hand hygiene, equipment sterilization, and limiting unnecessary catheter use reduce spread.

faq.q: Why does it cause green sputum?
faq.a: The pigment pyocyanin gives a greenish hue to secretions.

exam: Explain why Pseudomonas is a common pathogen in ventilator‑associated pneumonia and describe the first‑line treatment strategy.
Describe the role of biofilm in chronic Pseudomonas airway infection in cystic fibrosis and how it affects therapy.
List key infection control measures to prevent Pseudomonas transmission in a low‑resource hospital setting.
